prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "NOVO NORDISK A S" (ticker NVO), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "NVO", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Novo Nordisk A/S
markets: Obesity medicines (Wegovy injection and Wegovy pill, Saxenda)
Rare blood and rare endocrine disorders (haemophilia, growth hormone)

mission.statement: driving change to defeat serious chronic diseases
mission.source: Novo Nordisk Annual Report 2025, 'Purpose, strategy and culture' ("At Novo Nordisk, our purpose remains clear: driving change to defeat serious chronic diseases.")
mission.plain: Novo wants to beat long-lasting illnesses like diabetes and obesity, not just treat them.

about.plain: Novo Nordisk is a Danish company that makes medicines for people with diabetes and for people who need to lose weight. Its best-known medicines, Ozempic and Wegovy, are weekly shots (and now also a daily pill) that help control blood sugar and appetite. It has made insulin for over 100 years and also makes medicines for rare blood and growth problems. Most of its money comes from the United States.
about.customers: Pharmacies, hospitals, insurers and government health systems buy its medicines for patients, and more and more people also pay for weight-loss medicine themselves.
about.everyday: Ozempic and Wegovy are the 'weight-loss shots' people talk about on TV and social media.

money.plain: Ozempic shots and Rybelsus pills for type 2 diabetes
a daily weight-loss pill launched in the US in January 2026
CagriSema and amycretin, aiming for bigger weight loss

result.summary: Novo Nordisk invented the semaglutide medicines that created the modern obesity-drug market, and it still has huge manufacturing scale, 100 years of diabetes know-how and global reach. But its advantage has narrowed sharply: Eli Lilly's tirzepatide drugs now lead US prescriptions, semaglutide patents are expiring in some countries, and US prices are being cut, so its moat is real but weakening.

pricingPower.evidence: Novo is cutting rather than raising prices: under its Most Favoured Nations agreement with the US Administration it will lower the US list price of Wegovy to $675 a month (about -50%) and Ozempic to $675 (about -35%) from 1 January 2027, sells the Wegovy pill for $149-299 a month self-pay, and guides 2026 adjusted sales to fall 0-6% at constant exchange rates despite obesity patients treated rising 69% to 4.9 million (H1 2026).

moats.evidence: Ozempic and Wegovy are household names and the Wegovy pill holds about 90% of the US GLP-1 pill market (Aug 2026), but semaglutide patents have expired in markets such as Canada and China in 2026 and US exclusivity runs only to the early 2030s.
Patients and doctors can switch between GLP-1 brands with a new prescription, as the shift to Lilly's Zepbound and Mounjaro (about 61% of US incretin prescriptions per Lilly in 2026) shows.
A medicine does not become more valuable to one patient because others use it.

Novo spent DKK 60.1bn on plants in 2025 and bought Catalent's fill-finish sites (DKK 82.2bn acquisition cash outflow in 2024), giving it some of the world's largest peptide and injection capacity, though Lilly is building similar scale.
The global GLP-1 market is essentially a duopoly of Novo and Lilly because few firms can make peptides at this volume, although generic semaglutide and new entrants (Pfizer, Amgen, Roche) are coming.
Novo is the incumbent; it faces counter-positioning from telehealth sellers and cheaper generics rather than benefiting from it.

A century of insulin and peptide manufacturing know-how and the discovery of semaglutide are hard to copy, but the CagriSema head-to-head shortfall versus tirzepatide and failed trials (ziltivekimab ZEUS, July 2026) show its R&D edge has slipped.

Semaglutide patents (key US patent into the early 2030s) and control by the Novo Nordisk Foundation, which provides very stable long-term ownership, are exclusive assets, though the patents are time-limited.

customers.evidence: Demand is strong (over 5 million Wegovy pill prescriptions in the first seven months after its January 2026 launch and 46.5 million patients treated), but many patients have switched to Lilly's tirzepatide for greater weight loss and Novo lost US insulin share in Q2 2026.

talent.evidence: Novo has long been a top employer in Denmark and was named the World's Best Workplace by Fortune/Great Place to Work in 2022, but it cut its workforce from 77,349 (end-2024) to about 66,700 (mid-2026) in a company-wide restructuring, which hurt morale.

product.evidence: Semaglutide is proven, including cardiovascular benefits, and the Wegovy pill leads the oral GLP-1 market, but tirzepatide gives more weight loss and CagriSema met non-inferiority for weight but not HbA1c versus tirzepatide in REIMAGINE 4.

competitors.name: Eli Lilly and Company
competitors.note: Mounjaro, Zepbound and the Foundayo (orforglipron) pill compete head-on in diabetes and obesity; also insulin.

competitors.name: Pfizer
competitors.note: Entered obesity through its Metsera acquisition; also haemophilia gene and antibody therapies.

competitors.name: Amgen
competitors.note: MariTide, a monthly obesity antibody in phase 3.

competitors.name: Roche
competitors.note: Obesity pipeline (CT-388, petrelintide with Zealand Pharma) and haemophilia (Hemlibra).

competitors.name: Boehringer Ingelheim
competitors.note: Survodutide for obesity and MASH; Jardiance in diabetes (private).

competitors.name: Zealand Pharma
competitors.note: Amylin and GLP-1 obesity pipeline partnered with Roche.

competitors.name: Viking Therapeutics
competitors.note: VK2735 injectable and oral obesity candidates.

competitors.name: Hims & Hers Health
competitors.note: US telehealth seller of GLP-1 treatments, including compounded versions, competing for self-pay patients.

competitors.name: Sandoz
competitors.note: Generic semaglutide in markets where patents have expired (e.g. Canada).

competitors.name: Novartis
competitors.note: Cardiovascular and renal medicines that overlap with Novo's cardiorenal focus.

marketShare.market: US incretin (GLP-1) diabetes and obesity medicines
marketShare.measure: prescriptions (as reported by Eli Lilly, Aug 2026)

threats: Eli Lilly's tirzepatide (Mounjaro, Zepbound) and Foundayo pill taking share in the US and abroad
US price cuts: the MFN agreement and roughly 50% Wegovy / 35% Ozempic list-price cuts from January 2027, plus Medicare price negotiation of semaglutide
Semaglutide patent expiry and generics in Canada, China, Brazil, India and other markets from 2026, and in the US in the early 2030s
Pipeline setbacks: CagriSema underperformed tirzepatide, ziltivekimab failed the ZEUS trial (July 2026) and DKK 6.3bn of pipeline impairments in Q2 2026
Compounded and telehealth GLP-1 copies competing for self-pay patients
New obesity entrants (Pfizer/Metsera, Amgen MariTide, Roche/Zealand, Boehringer survodutide, Chinese makers)
Investor lawsuits over share losses and execution risk in the restructuring

ceo.name: Maziar Mike Doustdar
ceo.background: Iranian-born Austrian; BA in International Business (Webster University Vienna, 1994); joined Novo as an office clerk in Vienna in 1992 and ran International Operations from 2013 before becoming CEO in August 2025

c1.evidence: Novo pioneered the fast-growing obesity-drug industry (IQVIA branded obesity volume up 81% globally, MAT May 2026), but Eli Lilly now leads US incretin prescriptions with about 61%.

c2.evidence: Patients choose Novo for proven semaglutide with heart benefits, a first-to-market oral Wegovy pill (about 90% of US GLP-1 pill prescriptions) and lower self-pay prices, but tirzepatide's greater weight loss and expiring patents make the edge copyable.

c3.evidence: Ozempic and Wegovy are household names, but Novo Nordisk itself is less recognised than its brands and is no longer the default leader now that Lilly is ahead.

c4.evidence: Its purpose 'driving change to defeat serious chronic diseases' and the triple bottom line are central to the company, which is controlled by the non-profit Novo Nordisk Foundation; a decade of progress on obesity and diabetes would matter enormously.

c6.evidence: “Ozempic, weight-loss shots, Danish, struggling against Lilly” come to mind; the products are seen very positively, but the company's image has dimmed after profit warnings, layoffs and share-price falls.

c7.evidence: Almost 1 billion people live with obesity and around 600 million with diabetes, and obesity-drug volume grew 81% (MAT May 2026), a large secular trend.

c8.evidence: Semaglutide can expand into heart, kidney and liver disease and the company aims to reach more than 60 million patients by 2030, but in 2025 it dropped standalone expansion into CKD, cardiovascular disease and MASH to focus on obesity and diabetes.

m1.evidence: Doustdar has set clear 2030 goals (more than five blockbuster launches, DKK 150bn+ pipeline sales by 2035, 10x oral GLP-1 reach) but his agenda is mainly a commercial turnaround rather than a new vision.

m2.evidence: Doustdar is not a founder but a 33-year company lifer who rose from office clerk, and the Foundation's control encourages long-term thinking.

m4.evidence: He has emphasised patient access with cheap self-pay pricing ($149-299/month Wegovy pill) but also cut the workforce from 77,349 to about 66,700.

m5.evidence: The Novo Nordisk Way culture predates him; Doustdar is reshaping it toward speed and cost discipline, with mixed early results in innovation.

m6.evidence: Doustdar has a business degree and a career in commercial operations, not science or engineering.

m7.evidence: Novo's Foundation ownership and access programmes aim at broad health benefits, but there is no distinctive public record yet of Doustdar's personal stewardship beyond the company's mission.

m7b.evidence: No commencement speech by Doustdar at a top university was found.

m8b.evidence: Doustdar is known as a blunt, hard-driving operator but does not have a widely recognised public persona.

m9.evidence: He built International Operations into Novo's largest growth region (DKK 135.9bn sales in 2025), but since he became CEO in August 2025 the company has issued a 2026 sales-decline outlook and the shares have fallen.

m10.evidence: Doustdar launched a company-wide transformation costing about DKK 8bn in 2025 to cut costs, but Novo is not known for frugality.

c10.evidence: Novo medicines treated about 46.5 million people worldwide (MAT H1 2026), including 41.6 million with diabetes.

p2.evidence: Discovering and mass-producing peptide medicines like semaglutide at billions of doses requires deep science and huge sterile manufacturing capacity, and addresses major chronic diseases.

f1.evidence: Net sales rose every year from DKK 126,946m in 2020 to DKK 309,064m in 2025.

f2.evidence: Gross margin fell from 83.5% (2020) to 81.0% (2025) and operating margin from 42.6% to 41.3%.

f3.evidence: Equity is positive (DKK 221,277m at June 2026), but borrowings of DKK 140,127m far exceed cash and securities of DKK 44,982m, though debt is only about 1.2x 2025 operating cash flow of DKK 119,102m.

f4.evidence: Operating profit rose from DKK 54,126m (2020) to 127,658m (2025) and operating cash flow from DKK 51,951m to 119,102m, though both dipped slightly in 2025.

v1.evidence: Lilly's tirzepatide gives more weight loss than semaglutide and CagriSema did not beat it, so Novo's injectables are not clearly best, though its Wegovy pill leads oral treatment.

v2.evidence: Novo was named the World's Best Workplace in 2022 and is a top Danish employer, but large layoffs in 2025-26 have dented its reputation.

c5.evidence: Tens of millions of people relying on its insulin, GLP-1 and haemophilia medicines would miss it immediately, as Novo is one of only three major global insulin makers.
